description: I’m a cloud solution architect and Java/Python developer with a focus on AI, multi-agent systems, knowledge bases and observability. We’re building an astronaut health copilot: AI agents that watch health indicators, explain risks and recommend actions. It has a clickable body map, trend charts and a trace view of agent decisions. It uses open-source tools only (Streamlit, Ollama) for the purpose of this demo.
summary:
AstroGuard is health monitoring software for astronauts on long missions, where Earth can be minutes away and unreachable for weeks. On the way to the Moon or Mars, an astronaut who feels unwell can't wait for Earth: messages take minutes and contact can drop for weeks. AstroGuard puts health monitoring onboard, so every astronaut can understand their own health and act in time.

Each astronaut sees their own vitals, check-ins, 14-day trends and a clickable body map, with plain-language guidance on how to measure each reading in space, why it matters and what to do.

Astronauts ask in natural language, like "Why is my blood pressure rising?" An agentic AI assistant uses tools to check their data, trends and cabin air, searches NASA guidance and answers with sources, following the same need-to-know privacy rules as people.

A multi-agent system watches the crew continuously: five monitoring agents, a coordinator that separates cabin problems from personal ones, and a self-healing supervisor. In an emergency, the crew gets step-by-step guidance while a report goes to the ground.

A ground app keeps the flight surgeon in the loop over a delayed, store-and-forward link, and real Inspiration4 blood data from NASA OSDR (OSD-575) gives readings a spaceflight reference.
details:
**Live demo:** https://astroguard-a3xh.onrender.com (the first load may take up to a minute on free hosting; demo access codes are shown on the login screen)

**What it does**
- **Astronaut app:** personal sign-in; color-coded status and fit-for-duty; live wearable data plus daily check-ins (blood pressure, blood sugar, temperature, sleep, mood); 14-day trends; a clickable body map; routine reminders with points, streaks and badges.


- **Built for non-doctors:** every indicator explains how to measure it in space, why it matters (linked to NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight), the normal range and what to do. Recommendations are tiered: self-care, crew medical officer or flight surgeon.


- **AI assistant (✨ Ask AstroGuard):** docked on every screen. It checks the asker's vitals, trends and cabin air, searches a NASA-based knowledge base and cites sources. Its tools run with the asker's own permissions (privacy-aware AI). Red-flag symptoms are caught by fixed code, not the AI. With a Claude API key it uses Claude; the public demo runs the built-in rule-based assistant, so it works offline too.


- **Emergency mode:** step-by-step protocols (chest pain/collapse, low oxygen, radiation storm, fainting) and live patient vitals; an SBAR situation report is sent to the flight surgeon (written by an AI agent when Claude is enabled).


- **Two apps, one mission:** the spacecraft app (master database) and the ground app (replica) sync in store-and-forward batches over a delayed link (the Mars delay is shortened for the demo). The design is inspired by NASA's Delay/Disruption Tolerant Networking, and nothing is lost during a solar-conjunction blackout.


- **Real NASA data:** the Inspiration4 crew's blood chemistry (NASA OSDR OSD-575) is shown next to each astronaut's own values and drives knowledge-base passages the AI cites.


- **Device ingestion:** an API for smart shirts (like CSA's Bio-Monitor), fitness bands, glucometers and BP cuffs, live or batch, validated and de-duplicated.


- **Privacy following NASA practice:** medical data stays between the astronaut and the flight surgeon (Privacy Act, private medical conferences); there are two crew medical officers, as NASA requires; the commander and mission control see fit-for-duty only; an emergency unlocks vitals; astronauts see who viewed their data.


- **Multi-agent monitoring:** cardio, respiratory, sleep, radiation and environment agents plus a coordinator (root cause: cabin vs. person) and a self-healing supervisor, with an observability dashboard.

**Benefits and impact:** earlier detection, guidance without medical training, faster emergency response when the ground is minutes away, and privacy that encourages honest reporting. It's designed for Earth-independent operations, and the same offline, guided design could serve remote communities on Earth.

**How it's creative:** onboard-first instead of ground-dependent; AI that follows the same need-to-know rules as humans; a delayed-link architecture you can see in the demo; real NASA flight data as a personal reference.

**Tools:** Python 3 (standard library), SQLite, HTML/CSS/JavaScript, Canvas, SVG, the Anthropic Claude API (optional), GitHub and Render.

**Factors considered:** communication delay and blackouts; safety (rule-based detection, AI only advises); NASA medical privacy; astronauts aren't doctors; limited bandwidth; and the limits of a prototype (synthetic crew data, demo thresholds, not a medical device).
